summary.text: The counterexample is $n=800{,}322{,}180$: monotonicity of $\binom{2k+1}{k}$ forces $0\le c\le d<16$, leaving 136 index pairs. For each pair, the remainder after subtracting the two binomial terms is excluded as a sum of two squares either by its residue modulo $4,8,9$, or $16$, or because a prime congruent to $3\pmod 4$ occurs in it to an odd exponent.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
B_k=\binom{2k+1}{k}
\]
and let
\[
N=800{,}322{,}180.
\]
We will prove that there are no nonnegative integers \(a,b,c,d\), with \(a\le b\) and \(c\le d\), such that
\[
N=a^2+b^2+B_c+B_d. \tag{1}
\]
Consequently the number of such representations is \(a(N)=0\). Since \(N>1\), this is a counterexample to the conjecture that \(a(n)>0\) for every \(n>1\).

We use two elementary obstructions to an integer being a sum of two squares.

First, if a prime \(p\equiv3\pmod4\) divides a sum \(x^2+y^2\), then it divides both \(x\) and \(y\). Indeed, if, say, \(p\nmid y\), then \((xy^{-1})^2\equiv-1\pmod p\), which is impossible because \(-1\) is not a quadratic residue modulo a prime congruent to \(3\pmod4\). The same argument applies if the roles of \(x\) and \(y\) are exchanged. Thus \(p^2\mid x^2+y^2\), and after dividing by \(p^2\) one may repeat the argument. It follows that every prime \(p\equiv3\pmod4\) occurs to an even exponent in the prime factorization of a sum of two squares. In particular, if the exact exponent \(v_p(R)\) of such a prime in \(R\) is odd, then \(R\) is not a sum of two squares.

Second, we will use the following small congruence obstructions. The relevant square residues and sum-of-two-square residues are:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
m&\{x^2\bmod m\}&\{x^2+y^2\bmod m\}\\ \hline
4&\{0,1\}&\{0,1,2\}\\
8&\{0,1,4\}&\{0,1,2,4,5\}\\
9&\{0,1,4,7\}&\{0,1,2,4,5,7,8\}\\
16&\{0,1,4,9\}&\{0,1,2,4,5,8,9,10,13\}.
\end{array}
\]
These sets follow simply by squaring every residue class and then adding every pair of square residues. Therefore a sum of two squares cannot be congruent to \(3\pmod4\), \(6\pmod8\), either \(3\) or \(6\pmod9\), or \(12\pmod{16}\).

We next reduce (1) to a finite list of cases. The sequence \(B_k\) is nondecreasing. To see this, Pascal's identity gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
B_{k+1}
 &=\binom{2k+3}{k+1}\\
 &=\binom{2k+2}{k}+\binom{2k+2}{k+1}\\
 &\ge \binom{2k+2}{k+1}\\
 &=\binom{2k+1}{k}+\binom{2k+1}{k+1}\\
 &\ge \binom{2k+1}{k}=B_k.
\end{aligned}
\]
Direct evaluation gives
\[
B_{16}=\binom{33}{16}=1{,}166{,}803{,}110>N.
\]
If (1) held, all four terms on its right would be nonnegative, so \(B_d\le N\). Monotonicity therefore forces \(d<16\). Since \(c\le d\), we also have \(c<16\). Thus it is enough to examine the 136 pairs
\[
0\le c\le d\le15.
\]
The needed values of \(B_k\) are
\[
\begin{array}{c|rrrrrrrr}
k&0&1&2&3&4&5&6&7\\ \hline
B_k&1&3&10&35&126&462&1716&6435
\end{array}
\]
\[
\begin{array}{c|rrrrrrrr}
k&8&9&10&11&12&13&14&15\\ \hline
B_k&24310&92378&352716&1352078&5200300&20058300&77558760&300540195.
\end{array}
\]

For each admissible pair put
\[
R_{c,d}=N-B_c-B_d.
\]
Equation (1) would imply \(R_{c,d}=a^2+b^2\). The following table gives an obstruction for every pair. The notation is as follows:

* \(M(m,r)\) means that direct subtraction gives \(R_{c,d}\equiv r\pmod m\), where \(r\) is absent from the sum-of-two-square residue set modulo \(m\) displayed above.
* \(P(p,e)\) means that \(p\) is a prime with \(p\equiv3\pmod4\), and that \(p^e\mid R_{c,d}\) but \(p^{e+1}\nmid R_{c,d}\). Thus \(v_p(R_{c,d})=e\); every exponent \(e\) appearing below is odd.

Each row fixes \(c\), and each item has the form “\(d:\) obstruction.”

For completeness, all numerical assertions in this table are finite elementary calculations from the displayed list of \(B_k\). For an \(M(m,r)\) entry, one subtracts the two indicated \(B\)-values from \(N\) and reduces modulo \(m\). For a \(P(p,e)\) entry, division shows that \(p^e\) divides that same difference while one further factor of \(p\) does not. The distinct primes used are
\[
3,7,11,19,23,31,43,59,67,139,163,223,227,467,563,647,719,991,1999,2819,689891,12504647.
\]
Each is congruent to \(3\pmod4\). Their primality is checked by trial division by primes no larger than their square roots; no divisor occurs. Thus the labels \(P(p,e)\) provide exactly the odd-valuation obstruction proved at the start, rather than merely a divisibility assertion. As illustrations of how the table is read, for \((c,d)=(0,3)\),
\[
R_{0,3}=800322180-1-35=800322144\equiv6\pmod9,
\]
which is impossible for a sum of two squares. For \((c,d)=(4,10)\),
\[
R_{4,10}=800322180-126-352716=799969338,
\]
and \(3^3\mid799969338\) but \(3^4\nmid799969338\), so the prime \(3\equiv3\pmod4\) has odd exact exponent. The other entries are interpreted identically.

Now suppose (1) held. We already showed that its ordered indices would satisfy \(0\le c\le d\le15\), so its pair \((c,d)\) occurs in the table. If that entry is \(M(m,r)\), reducing \(a^2+b^2=R_{c,d}\) modulo \(m\) contradicts the listed sum-of-two-square residues. If it is \(P(p,e)\), then \(R_{c,d}\) contains the prime \(p\equiv3\pmod4\) to an odd exact exponent, contradicting the necessary even-exponent property of a sum of two squares. Thus every possible pair is impossible. This proves that \(N\) has no representation of the required form. Notice that the condition \(a\le b\) does not need any additional treatment: the argument has actually ruled out all choices of \(a,b\), whether ordered or not.

Finally, by definition, \(a(N)\) counts precisely the quadruples of nonnegative integers satisfying the two order conditions and equation (1). Since there are no such quadruples, every contribution to that count is zero, and hence
\[
a(800322180)=0.
\]
But \(800322180>1\). Therefore the assertion “for every integer \(n>1\), \(a(n)>0\)” is false.
